summary: Updates the Teredo IPv6-over-IPv4 tunneling protocol by changing how the flags field embedded in every Teredo address is used. The changes improve security while staying backward compatible with existing implementations.

eli5.summary: Teredo addresses carry a little set of switches. This document changes how those switches are used so that outsiders find it harder to misuse them, while old equipment still works.

subtitle: Randomizing bits in Teredo addresses and retiring the cone bit so attackers have a harder time scanning.

tldr.problem: Teredo IPv6 addresses are structured and partly predictable, so an attacker who knows a client's mapped IPv4 address and port could scan for its IPv6 address. The cone bit also hints at how open the client's NAT is.
tldr.mechanism: Clients fill 12 unused bits of the 16-bit Flags field with random values, which multiplies the search space by 4,096. Clients also skip the first qualification phase and ignore the cone bit in peers' addresses.
tldr.outcome: Teredo stays backward compatible while becoming harder to scan and less revealing about the NAT. It updates RFC 4380.

facts.label: Addresses to try per IPv4 address/port

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Teredo (RFC 4380) lets hosts behind NATs reach the IPv6 Internet by embedding data in a special IPv6 address. This document updates RFC 4380 with two security changes to the Flags field of that address. Both are backward compatible.

The Flags field has 16 bits, of which 13 are unused. The first change randomizes 12 of those 13 bits. The second deprecates the cone bit, which tells a peer whether it must send Teredo control messages before communicating.
sections.eli5: Teredo addresses have a small set of switches, and most of them were never used. This document puts the unused ones to work to keep outsiders guessing.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
The RFC defines the NAT behaviours it relies on. A cone NAT maps all requests from one internal address and port to the same external address and port, and any external host can send to it. A restricted NAT uses the same mapping but only lets an external host send after the internal host has first sent to it.

The mapped address/port is the global IPv4 address and UDP port that results from NAT translation. An indirect bubble is a Teredo control message sent to another client via that client's Teredo server.
sections.eli5: A cone NAT is a front door anyone can knock on once you have opened it. A restricted NAT only opens for people you have already called.

sections.title: Random Address Flags
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the fields of a Teredo address and how guessable each one is. The 32-bit Teredo prefix has a single IANA-assigned value. The 32-bit server field is usually statically configured, so attackers can limit guesses to popular servers. The 16-bit client port depends on the chosen service port and NAT behaviour, and can be predictable if NATs are port-preserving. The 32-bit client IPv4 address can be narrowed down if an attacker knows the target organization, and some ranges may hold many Teredo clients.

The Flags layout becomes C|z|Random1|U|G|Random2. The z flag stays reserved and MUST be zero. Random1 and Random2 MUST be set to random values. C, U and G are as in RFC 4380, with the use of C modified by the next section.
sections.eli5: Some parts of the address were easy to guess, like which post office and which street. The new random digits are a secret part of the house number that guessers have to find by trial and error.

sections.title: Deprecating the Cone Bit
sections.content:
The cone bit may reveal the security posture of a network. If it is set, an attacker may decide it is worth port-scanning the embedded IPv4 address and others from the same organization.

Teredo clients SHOULD skip the first phase of the qualification procedure and run only the second phase, using the Teredo link-local address with the cone bit set to zero. Cone and restricted NATs can then no longer be told apart. Communication still works, but peers skip case 4 of the sending details in RFC 4380, so the same number of indirect bubbles is sent as for a peer behind a restricted NAT. Clients and relays SHOULD also ignore the cone bit in a peer's address and treat it as clear.

Teredo servers MUST NOT ignore the cone bit. It controls which IPv4 source address the server uses when answering a Router Solicitation, and legacy clients would wrongly conclude they are behind a cone NAT and lose connectivity. The server's own address also keeps its cone bit set.
sections.eli5: Before, the address showed whether your front door was easy to open, which told burglars where to try. Now everyone acts as if the door is the careful kind, which is slightly slower but gives nothing away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goal stated for Teredo is that a client should be as secure as a host attached directly to an untrusted Internet link. The random bits protect against IPv6 address scanning by off-path attackers: even knowing the mapped IPv4 address and port, an attacker must try a range of 4,096 IPv6 addresses.

The random bits MUST be generated following the recommendations in the NIST random number generation document and RFC 4086. The RFC also says Teredo is NOT RECOMMENDED for networks that want strict control over traffic crossing the Internet boundary, and administrators of such networks may wish to filter all Teredo traffic at their borders.
sections.eli5: If the random digits are easy to guess they do not help, so they must come from a good random source. Strict networks may simply decide not to allow Teredo at all.

sections.title: Implementation Status and Address Prediction
sections.content:
Appendix A states that the cone bit deprecation is implemented in Windows Vista and Windows Server 2008, and the random flags in Windows Vista SP1 and Windows Server 2008. Windows implementations automatically disable Teredo on a managed network with a domain controller.

Appendix B compares address guessing to SLAAC. If the attacker knows the external IPv4 address, the unknown port (16 bits) and random bits (12 bits) give a 28-bit search space. That compares favorably with the 24 bits needed for a SLAAC address when the Ethernet vendor is known. Without the random bits the space would be only 16 bits.
sections.eli5: Adding the random digits makes guessing about as hard as it is for ordinary IPv6 addresses. Without them, guessing would be far easier.
